content: Cystic fibrosis is the most prevalent autosomal recessive disorder in white populations and is associated with significant respiratory dysfunction in most affected individuals. Various forms of respiratory muscle training (RMT), including inspiratory and expiratory muscle training, have been explored in the literature as potential interventions to improve respiratory function and health-related quality of life in individuals with cystic fibrosis. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of RMT on clinical outcomes in this population. This review is an update of a previously published analysis. The objective of the review was to assess the impact of RMT on clinical outcomes in individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was performed using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches and manual searches of relevant journals and conference proceedings. The most recent search of the database was conducted on June 11, 2020, and an additional search of the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis, Pediatric Pulmonology, and online trial databases was completed on October 5, 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared RMT interventions with control groups in individuals with cystic fibrosis. The authors independently selected studies for inclusion, assessed their methodological quality, and extracted relevant data. When necessary, additional information was requested from the trial authors. The quality of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. A total of 20 studies were identified, of which 10 studies involving 238 participants met the inclusion criteria. The methodological and reporting quality of the included studies varied significantly. Four of the 10 studies were published only as abstracts and lacked detailed information, limiting the available data. Eight studies employed a parallel design, while two used a crossover design. The RMT interventions varied widely in terms of frequency (three times per week to twice daily), intensity (20% to 80% of maximal effort), and duration (10 to 30 minutes per session). The sample sizes of the included studies ranged from 11 to 39 participants. Five studies focused exclusively on adults, one on children, and four included both children and adults. The primary outcomes assessed were pulmonary function (measured by forced expiratory volume in one second [FEV1] and forced vital capacity [FVC]) and postural stability. No significant differences were observed between the treatment and control groups for these outcomes, and the evidence was of very low quality. Exercise capacity, as measured by maximum oxygen consumption and distance covered in a six-minute walk test, also showed no significant changes. However, one study (n = 20) reported a 10% improvement in exercise duration when participants worked at 60% of maximal effort (very low-quality evidence). Another study (n = 18) found improvements in health-related quality of life in the mastery and emotion domains when participants worked at 80% of maximal effort (very low-quality evidence). Regarding secondary outcomes, one study (n = 11) reported changes in intramural pressure, functional residual capacity, and maximal inspiratory pressure following RMT (very low-quality evidence). Another study (n = 36) demonstrated significant improvements in maximal inspiratory pressure after training (P < 0.001, very low-quality evidence). Additionally, a study (n = 22) found that respiratory muscle endurance was significantly longer in the training group (P < 0.01). No significant differences were reported for other secondary outcomes. Due to inconsistencies and insufficient detail in the reported outcome measures, meta-analyses could not be performed. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether RMT is beneficial for individuals with cystic fibrosis. Healthcare practitioners should consider the use of RMT on a case-by-case basis. Further high-quality research is needed to establish the effectiveness of RMT in this population. Future studies should focus on clinical outcomes such as respiratory muscle function, pulmonary function, exercise capacity, hospital admissions, and health-related quality of life. Additionally, sensory-perceptual changes, such as perceived respiratory effort and peripheral exertion, may provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the potential benefits of RMT.
